title: Next-Gen Unmanned Aerial Target System
type: Full and open competition · best-value tradeoff · FAR Part 15
role: You are the Source Selection Authority (SSA). Work the source selection phase by phase. Each call carries a protest-risk cost when you get it wrong — the running score decides whether your award survives a GAO protest.
sourceNote: Ported from a colleague's warrant-prep exercise and rebuilt on the DoD Source Selection Procedures (Aug 2022). Every rule below deep-links to the governing SSP or FAR-Overhaul section.

offerors.name: AeroDyne Systems
offerors.note: Two significant strengths — proprietary radar-absorbent polymer and advanced SOC integration. Delivered the MQ-99 target system.

offerors.name: GlobalTech Corp
offerors.note: Meets requirements; one weakness (no tertiary flight failsafe) resolved in discussions. Strong commercial drone record, no military EW experience.

offerors.name: Horizon Dynamics

ratingCite.quote: Blue — Outstanding — Proposal demonstrates an exceptional approach and understanding of the requirements, contains multiple strengths and/or at least one significant strength.

ratingNote: Ratings use SSP Methodology 1 (Table 2A/2B): the technical adjectival rating and the technical-risk rating are assigned separately — which is why each offeror reads as "rating / risk" (e.g. Outstanding / Low).

pws.title: Performance Work Statement (PWS)
pws.html:
CUI // Source Selection Information — see FAR 2.101 and 3.104

Performance Work Statement (PWS)

Next-Gen Unmanned Aerial Target System (NG-UATS)

1.0 Scope and background:
The Department of the Air Force requires the design, development, integration, test, and delivery of a stealth-capable unmanned aerial target drone. This Next-Gen Unmanned Aerial Target System (NG-UATS) will simulate fifth-generation adversary fighter aircraft for live-fire air-to-air and surface-to-air missile testing. The contractor shall provide all personnel, equipment, supplies, facilities, transportation, tools, materials, supervision, and other items necessary to perform this requirement.

2.0 Applicable documents:
- MIL-STD-810H: Environmental Engineering Considerations
- DoD Instruction 8500.01: Cybersecurity
- AFMAN 14-403: Cybersecurity Risk Management Framework (RMF)

3.0 Technical requirements:
3.1 Flight kinematics & autonomy: The NG-UATS must achieve a minimum speed of Mach 0.95 and sustain 8G maneuvers. The system must possess autonomous threat ingestion, dynamically altering its flight path to evade radar lock without ground control intervention.
3.2 Cyber resilience (critical): The platform must integrate with the 24/7 Security Operations Center (SOC). All telemetry and command links must be encrypted using NSA-approved Suite B cryptography (AES-256 minimum). The system must withstand Level 4 penetration testing.
3.3 Payload & modularity: The airframe must support a modular payload bay with a minimum capacity of 500 lbs to accommodate various electronic warfare (EW) pods, scoring acoustics, and chaff/flare dispensers.

4.0 Deliverables (CDRLs):
The contractor shall deliver ten (10) NG-UATS prototype units, two (2) Ground Control Stations (GCS), and a comprehensive Level III Technical Data Package (TDP).

igce.title: Independent Government Cost Estimate (IGCE)
igce.html:
CUI // Source Selection Information — see FAR 2.101 and 3.104

Independent Government Cost Estimate (IGCE)

Program: NG-UATS · Date: 01-SEP-202X

1.0 Methodology:
This IGCE was developed using a hybrid estimating methodology. The airframe and propulsion estimates are based on parametric modeling drawn from the legacy MQ-107 and BQM-167 programs, adjusted for inflation and a 15% complexity factor for stealth composites. The software and cyber integration components were developed using a bottom-up Subject Matter Expert (SME) engineering build-up based on estimated lines of code (SLOC).

2.0 Work breakdown structure (WBS) estimate:

WBS elementDescriptionLabor/mat. mixEstimated cost
1.0System Engineering & Program Mgmt (SEPM)80% L / 20% M$20,000,000
2.0Airframe & Propulsion (R&D)40% L / 60% M$100,000,000
3.0Avionics & Cyber Security Integration90% L / 10% M$45,000,000
4.0Low Rate Initial Production (LRIP) — 10 units30% L / 70% M$85,000,000
Total estimated cost:$250,000,000

3.0 Assumptions & escalation:
Rates are escalated at 2.5% annually. Direct labor rates were validated against current DCMA Forward Pricing Rate Agreements (FPRAs) for major aerospace contractors. Materials estimates assume no supply chain disruptions for rare-earth metals.

D. Smith, Chief Cost Estimator

ap.title: Acquisition Plan (AP)
ap.html:
CUI // Source Selection Information — see FAR 2.101 and 3.104

Formal Acquisition Plan (FAR Part 7)

Program: NG-UATS

1. Statement of need: The NG-UATS addresses a critical capability gap identified in the 202X National Defense Strategy. Current target drones cannot replicate the radar cross-section or kinematic profiles of near-peer adversary aircraft, rendering our live-fire testing inadequate.

2. Acquisition strategy:
2.1 Competition: Full and open competition under FAR Part 15. No set-asides are appropriate due to the manufacturing complexity and capital requirements, though small business subcontracting plans will be heavily evaluated.
2.2 Contract type: A hybrid contract vehicle is authorized. CLIN 0001 (R&D / software integration) will be Cost-Plus-Incentive-Fee (CPIF) to absorb developmental risk. CLIN 0002 (production of 10 prototypes) will be Firm-Fixed-Price (FFP).
2.3 Source selection procedures: A best-value subjective tradeoff process will be utilized in accordance with DoD Source Selection Procedures.

3. Program risks: Primary risks involve cyber-vulnerability of the datalink and weight integration. Mitigation involves stringent Section M evaluation criteria for system architecture.

Approved: Head of Contracting Activity (HCA)

risk.title: Pre-RFP Risk Assessment
risk.html:
CUI // Source Selection Information — see FAR 2.101 and 3.104

Pre-Solicitation Risk Assessment Report

1. Purpose: To identify programmatic risks prior to RFP release to ensure Section L (Instructions) and Section M (Evaluation Factors) adequately capture and evaluate vendor mitigation strategies.

Risk IDDescriptionLikelihoodConsequenceMitigation strategy for RFP
R-01Cyber hijacking of command linkModerateCatastrophicCreate distinct evaluation subfactor (1.2). Require Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) and proof of AES-256 capability in Section L.
R-02Payload weight exceedanceHighCriticalRequire 3D CAD modeling and detailed weight-and-balance buildup charts in the Technical Volume.
R-03Supply chain delays (composites)ModerateModerateRequire a detailed Supply Chain Risk Management (SCRM) plan in the Past Performance / Management volume.

2. Conclusion: Technical risks heavily outweigh cost risks. Therefore, the Source Selection Plan must state that Technical is significantly more important than Price.

ssp.title: Source Selection Plan (SSP)
ssp.html:
CUI // Source Selection Information — see FAR 2.101 and 3.104

Source Selection Plan (SSP)

Program: NG-UATS · Authority: FAR 15.3 / DoD SSP

1. Organization:
- SSA: Col. Vance, Commander
- PCO: Lead Contracting Officer
- SSAC Chair: Ms. Jenkins, Director of Operations
- SSEB Chair: Dr. Aris, Chief Engineer

2. Evaluation factors & subfactors:
Factor 1: Technical (separate technical and risk ratings — SSP Methodology 1)
  Subfactor 1.1: System Architecture & Kinematics
  Subfactor 1.2: Cyber Integration & Resilience
Factor 2: Past Performance (confidence assessment)
Factor 3: Cost/Price

3. Relative importance:
Subfactor 1.1 and 1.2 are of equal importance. Factor 1 (Technical) is significantly more important than Factor 2 (Past Performance). Factor 1 and Factor 2, when combined, are significantly more important than Factor 3 (Cost/Price). This establishes a clear best-value tradeoff continuum.

4. Rating methodology:
Technical ratings follow the DoD SSP definitions: Blue (Outstanding), Purple (Good), Green (Acceptable), Yellow (Marginal), Red (Unacceptable). Technical risk is rated Low / Moderate / High / Unacceptable.

SSA approval signature

rfi.title: Market Research: RFI & Industry Day
rfi.html:
CUI // Source Selection Information — see FAR 2.101 and 3.104

Market Research & Industry Day Memorandum

1. Overview: On 12 October, an Industry Day was hosted at the installation. 45 industry representatives attended, including major defense primes and non-traditional mid-tier tech firms. A draft PWS was circulated via SAM.gov as a Request for Information (RFI).

2. Summary of industry feedback:

  • AeroDyne Systems: Requested clarification on the stealth coating maintenance requirements.
  • GlobalTech Corp: Submitted a formal white paper demonstrating that the mandatory 450 lb payload requirement prevents the use of Commercial Off-The-Shelf (COTS) high-density batteries, which would force a custom battery redesign and add $20M to development costs.
  • Horizon Dynamics: Requested a 30-day extension to the proposed RFP response time.

3. Government action: Based on the GlobalTech feedback and subsequent Government engineering review, the PM decided to change the PWS payload requirement from 450 lbs to 500 lbs. This change does not impact mission efficacy but increases the pool of viable competitors, allows the use of commercial products, and reduces cost.

compliance.html:

Proposal Compliance Review Matrix

1. Purpose: The PCO conducted an initial compliance review against the instructions outlined in RFP Section L prior to releasing the volumes to the SSEB.

2. Findings:

  • AeroDyne: Passed. All page limits, margins, and formatting rules strictly followed. SF33 is signed.
  • GlobalTech: Passed. Cost volume models are fully unlocked and executable as required. SF33 is signed.
  • Horizon Dynamics: Issue identified. Section L required all text, including tables and charts, to be in 12-point Times New Roman font. Horizon Dynamics utilized 10-point Arial font for five complex architectural diagrams in Volume I.

3. PCO determination: Regarding the Horizon Dynamics formatting issue, the 10-point font does not circumvent the page limit (the diagrams take up the same physical space) and does not afford Horizon an unfair competitive advantage.

tech_ind.title: SSEB Individual Tech Reports
tech_ind.html:
CUI // Source Selection Information — see FAR 2.101 and 3.104

Evaluator Worksheet (excerpt)

Evaluator: #4 · Subfactor: 1.1 Architecture

Offeror: GlobalTech Corp

Evaluator notes:
Reviewing GlobalTech's Volume I, Page 45. They propose a dual-redundant flight control processor. While a dual system meets the literal text of the ‘Acceptable’ threshold in Section M, the PWS clearly details that this drone will endure violent 8G evasive maneuvers. In my professional engineering judgment, a dual-redundant system without a tertiary failsafe presents a measurable risk of total system failure during these maneuvers.

Proposed finding: Weakness.
Risk rating: Moderate. The proposed approach meets requirements but introduces a risk of disrupted schedule or degraded performance.

Offeror: AeroDyne Systems
Evaluator notes: Reviewing AeroDyne Vol I. Their proprietary radar-absorbent polymer drastically reduces the cross-section beyond our threshold requirement, greatly enhancing training realism.
Proposed finding: Significant strength.

tech_con.title: SSEB Technical Consensus Report
tech_con.html:
CUI // Source Selection Information — see FAR 2.101 and 3.104

SSEB Technical Consensus Report

1. Methodology: The SSEB met from 20-NOV to 25-NOV. All individual evaluators discussed their findings to reach a unified consensus rating for each offeror.

OfferorFactor 1 rating / riskConsensus findings justification
AeroDyneOutstanding / LowProposal contains 2 significant strengths (radar-absorbent polymer, advanced SOC integration). 0 weaknesses. Risk of unsuccessful performance is very low.
GlobalTechAcceptable / ModerateProposal meets requirements. 1 weakness identified (lack of tertiary flight failsafe). The SSEB consensus determined this introduces a moderate risk of failure during 8G maneuvers.
HorizonMarginal / High1 deficiency. Proposal explicitly failed to include AES-256 encryption on the telemetry datalink, proposing outdated AES-128 instead. This fails a mandatory PWS requirement.

2. SSEB Chair remarks: Horizon's deficiency in encryption is systemic to their entire software architecture. Correcting this would require a major rewrite of Volume I.

cost.title: Cost/Price Analysis Report
cost.html:
CUI // Source Selection Information — see FAR 2.101 and 3.104

Cost & Price Analysis Report

Prepared by: Pricing Directorate

1. Overview: The pricing team conducted a price analysis on the FFP CLINs to ensure reasonableness, and a cost realism analysis on the CPIF CLINs to ensure the offerors understand the work.

2. Analysis by offeror:

  • AeroDyne ($255,000,000): Evaluated price is 2% above the IGCE ($250M). Comparison against historical models shows the pricing is fair and reasonable. Cost realism analysis confirms labor mix is appropriate for the proposed technical approach.
  • GlobalTech ($210,000,000): Evaluated price is 16% below the IGCE. A detailed cost realism analysis was performed to ensure they are not ‘buying in.’ DCAA rate checks confirm their overhead and direct labor rates match their Forward Pricing Rate Agreement (FPRA). The savings stem from their use of existing commercial supply chains. Price is realistic and reasonable.
  • Horizon ($205,000,000): Unbalanced pricing identified. Year 1 production CLINs are heavily front-loaded, while out-year sustainment is priced at $1. Furthermore, the low cost reflects their failure to price the required AES-256 cyber encryption modules.

cr_brief.title: Competitive Range Decision Brief
cr_brief.html:
CUI // Source Selection Information — see FAR 2.101 and 3.104

Competitive Range Briefing to the SSA

Purpose: Brief Col. Vance (SSA) on initial evaluations and recommend the competitive range.

Evaluation roll-up:
- AeroDyne: Outstanding / Substantial Confidence / $255M
- GlobalTech: Acceptable / Satisfactory Confidence / $210M
- Horizon: Marginal / Satisfactory Confidence / $205M

PCO recommendation: Establish a competitive range of the most highly rated proposals.

Rationale: The competitive range must consist of the most highly rated proposals. Horizon received a Marginal rating due to a critical deficiency (missing AES-256). Curing this deficiency would require Horizon to completely re-architect their software baseline, constituting a major proposal rewrite. They have no reasonable chance of award.

crdd.title: Competitive Range Decision Document
crdd.html:
CUI // Source Selection Information — see FAR 2.101 and 3.104

Competitive Range Determination Document (CRDD)

1. Determination: Based on the initial evaluation reports of the SSEB and the Cost/Price team, I have determined that the proposals submitted by AeroDyne Systems and GlobalTech Corp are the most highly rated and have a reasonable chance of being selected for award.

I further determine that the proposal submitted by Horizon Dynamics is excluded from the competitive range. Their technical approach contained a major deficiency regarding cyber encryption that cannot be corrected without a major proposal rewrite. Their pricing was also found to be unbalanced.

2. Direction: The PCO is directed to notify Horizon Dynamics of their exclusion, offer a pre-award debriefing, and open formal discussions with AeroDyne and GlobalTech.

Col Vance, SSA

ens.title: Evaluation Notices (ENs)
ens.html:
CUI // Source Selection Information — see FAR 2.101 and 3.104

Evaluation Notices (ENs) Issued

The following formal letters were issued to vendors in the competitive range to open discussions:

To: AeroDyne Systems
EN-01 (Clarification): In Vol I, Page 12, paragraph 3, the delivery date for Prototype #3 references ‘Month 14,’ but the master schedule on Page 15 indicates ‘Month 16.’ Please clarify the intended delivery timeline. No other weaknesses or deficiencies were noted.

To: GlobalTech Corp
EN-01 (Weakness / Moderate Risk): Reference RFP Section M, Subfactor 1.1; GlobalTech Vol I, Page 45. Your proposal details a dual-redundant flight control system. The Government evaluated this as a weakness. Because the PWS requires 8G evasion maneuvers, a dual-redundant system lacking a tertiary failsafe introduces a moderate risk of catastrophic mission failure if the primary and secondary systems encounter a G-lock fault. Please address how GlobalTech will mitigate this risk, and provide updated pricing if your technical approach changes.

en_eval.title: Pre-FPR EN Evaluation
en_eval.html:
CUI // Source Selection Information — see FAR 2.101 and 3.104

Interim Evaluation of EN Responses

1. Purpose: To determine if meaningful discussions have concluded and if the Government is ready to request Final Proposal Revisions (FPRs).

2. SSEB findings on responses:

AeroDyne: AeroDyne confirmed that ‘Month 14’ was a typographical error and the master schedule of Month 16 is accurate. Clarification accepted.

GlobalTech: GlobalTech submitted a 15-page response to EN-01. They have agreed to redesign their architecture to include a tertiary failsafe processor. They provided updated schematics and software logic models. The SSEB Chief Engineer reviewed the update and determined it fully mitigates the G-lock risk. The weakness is successfully resolved.

3. PCO conclusion: All weaknesses and risks have been discussed. The PCO recommends closing discussions.

car.title: Comparative Analysis Report (CAR)
car.html:
CUI // Source Selection Information — see FAR 2.101 and 3.104

SSAC Comparative Analysis Report (CAR)

1. Purpose: The Source Selection Advisory Council (SSAC) has compared the final evaluations of AeroDyne and GlobalTech to provide a recommendation to the SSA.

2. Comparative analysis:
Technical/risk: AeroDyne (‘Outstanding’) is vastly superior to GlobalTech (‘Acceptable’). AeroDyne's proprietary radar-absorbent polymer significantly reduces radar cross-section beyond the threshold, allowing for far more realistic training for fifth-generation fighter pilots. GlobalTech meets the minimum threshold but offers no enhanced capabilities.
Past performance: AeroDyne (‘Substantial’) is superior to GlobalTech (‘Satisfactory’) due to AeroDyne's direct experience delivering military target drones.
Price: GlobalTech ($202M) is significantly cheaper than AeroDyne ($245M), representing a difference of $43M (17.5%).

3. Recommendation: The SSP explicitly states Technical is significantly more important than Price. The SSAC unanimously recommends that the $43M price premium is justified by AeroDyne's advanced stealth capabilities and lower performance risk, which directly translates to superior warfighter training.

ssdd.title: Source Selection Decision Document (SSDD)
ssdd.html:
CUI // Source Selection Information — see FAR 2.101 and 3.104

Source Selection Decision Document (SSDD)

Program: NG-UATS

1. Introduction: As the Source Selection Authority (SSA) for the NG-UATS program, I have independently reviewed the SSEB evaluations, the Cost/Price analysis, and the SSAC Comparative Analysis Report. This document sets forth my rationale for the final award decision.

2. Assessment of proposals: AeroDyne Systems submitted an ‘Outstanding’ technical proposal with ‘Substantial’ past performance at an evaluated price of $245,000,000. GlobalTech Corp submitted an ‘Acceptable’ technical proposal with ‘Satisfactory’ past performance at an evaluated price of $202,000,000.

3. Tradeoff analysis & decision: In accordance with the Source Selection Plan, technical capability is significantly more important than price. GlobalTech represents an acceptable, low-cost baseline. However, AeroDyne's technical approach contains two significant strengths. Specifically, their radar-absorbent polymer will allow Air Force pilots to train against a target that accurately mimics modern near-peer threats, a capability GlobalTech lacks. Furthermore, AeroDyne's proven track record on the MQ-99 program essentially eliminates schedule risk.

I have quantified this operational advantage and determined that the technical superiority and reduced risk offered by AeroDyne warrant the $43,000,000 price premium over GlobalTech. AeroDyne represents the best value to the Government.

4. Award: I direct the PCO to award the NG-UATS contract to AeroDyne Systems.

Col Vance, SSA

phases.title: Acquisition planning
phases.hat: Establish the source selection strategy in the SSP.
phases.prompt: What evaluation strategy will you establish in the SSP for this complex developmental system?

options.label: Best-value tradeoff — technical is significantly more important than price.

feedback.tradeoff: Right call. A stealth developmental system with high performance risk and a real need to pay for superior capability sits on the tradeoff end of the best-value continuum.
feedback.lpta: Wrong tool. LPTA is appropriate only where requirements are well defined, risk is minimal, and there is no value in paying for higher performance — the opposite of this program. Choosing it here will haunt your award decision in Phase 9.

cites.quote: At one end of the continuum, LPTA is appropriate where: requirements are well defined; risk of unsuccessful contract performance is minimal; and there is no value, need, or willingness to pay for higher performance.

phases.title: Market research
phases.hat: Review industry feedback before releasing the RFP.
phases.prompt: Industry states the 450 lb payload requirement restricts competition and forces a costly custom redesign. Do you amend the PWS?

feedback.relax: Good application of market research. Industry engagement surfaced a needlessly restrictive requirement; relaxing it broadens competition and lowers cost without hurting the mission.
feedback.strict: Retaining a requirement your own market research shows is restrictive — with no mission justification — needlessly limits competition and invites challenge.

cites.quote: Thorough and complete market research is the foundation of an effective source selection process.

phases.title: Receipt & security
phases.prompt: One SSEB evaluator disclosed they personally own $15,000 in AeroDyne stock. What do you do?

options.label: Remove the evaluator from the SSEB before they access any source selection information.
Keep the evaluator but ask them to stay objective.

feedback.remove: Integrity maintained. A direct personal financial interest is a conflict that must be resolved before the evaluator touches any source selection information — not managed with a promise.
feedback.keep: Fatal error. A direct financial stake in an offeror is exactly the conflict the NDA/COI review exists to catch. Leaving that evaluator on the board taints the entire evaluation and hands a protester an easy win.

cites.quote: actual or potential conflict of interest issues are resolved prior to granting access to any source selection information

phases.title: Compliance review
phases.hat: Screen proposals against Section L before the SSEB evaluates.
phases.prompt: Horizon used 10-point Arial instead of the required 12-point font on five diagrams. Page limits were still met and no advantage was gained. What do you do?

options.label: Accept the proposal — it's a minor informality.
Reject the proposal entirely for non-compliance with Section L.

feedback.accept: Correct. A formatting deviation that neither circumvents the page limit nor confers a competitive advantage is a minor informality the Government may waive.
feedback.reject: Overly rigid. Rejecting a compliant-in-substance proposal over a font size — with no page-limit gain and no advantage — is the kind of hyper-technical exclusion a protest will sustain.

cites.quote: The Government may waive informalities and minor irregularities in proposals received.

phases.title: Competitive range
phases.hat: Decide who stays in the competition.
phases.prompt: Horizon has a Marginal rating and a deficiency that would require a complete proposal rewrite to cure. Do you include them in the competitive range?

options.label: Eliminate Horizon — AeroDyne and GlobalTech remain.
Retain Horizon to keep maximum competition.

feedback.eliminate: Correct. The competitive range is the most highly rated proposals. A Marginal offeror with an uncurable-without-rewrite deficiency has no reasonable chance of award and does not belong in it.
feedback.keep: Retaining a proposal with no reasonable chance of award wastes Government and vendor resources and misapplies the competitive-range standard.

cites.quote: establish the competitive range based on the ratings of each proposal against all evaluation criteria

phases.title: Discussions
phases.hat: Issue Evaluation Notices to resolve weaknesses.
phases.prompt: How do you phrase the EN to GlobalTech about their missing tertiary failsafe?

options.label: A specific EN identifying the weakness and its risk, without prescribing the fix.
A general note: "Your flight system is weak. Please fix it."

feedback.tailored: Meaningful discussions. You told the offeror what was wrong and why it matters — enough to respond — without designing their solution for them.
feedback.vague: A vague EN fails the requirement to conduct meaningful discussions: the offeror can't tell what to fix, and the record won't show you disclosed the weakness.

cites.quote: the PCO must conduct and document meaningful discussions

phases.title: Final proposal revisions
phases.prompt: You've requested FPRs due in one week. AeroDyne calls and asks for two extra weeks. What do you do?

options.label: Grant the two weeks to BOTH offerors.
Grant the two weeks only to AeroDyne; GlobalTech's FPR is still due today.

feedback.equal: Equal treatment preserved. FPRs are due on a common cutoff date and time — a schedule accommodation must extend to everyone in the competitive range.
feedback.unequal: Unequal discussions. Extending the deadline for one offeror and not the other is a textbook prejudicial disparity that will sustain a protest.

cites.quote: each offeror still within the competitive range shall be given an opportunity to submit a FPR by a common cutoff date and time, as established by the PCO

phases.title: Cost realism
phases.hat: Evaluate the final prices before the tradeoff.
phases.prompt: GlobalTech dropped their final price by $8M. CLIN 0001 (the R&D effort) is CPIF. What must you do before the SSAC compares proposals?

options.label: Run a cost realism analysis to confirm the lower price is genuine, not a buy-in.
Accept the lower price — the Government loves savings.

feedback.realism: Correct. The developmental CLIN is cost-reimbursement (CPIF), so a cost realism analysis is required to determine what the Government should realistically expect to pay and whether the offeror understands the work.
feedback.blind: Accepting a lowered price on a cost-reimbursement CLIN without a realism analysis risks paying for an unrealistic bid — the classic buy-in the analysis exists to catch.

cites.quote: When contracting on a cost-reimbursement basis, evaluations shall include a cost realism analysis to determine what the Government should realistically expect to pay for the proposed effort

phases.title: Source selection decision
phases.hat: Make the tradeoff and sign the SSDD.
phases.prompt: AeroDyne is Outstanding but costs $43M more. GlobalTech is Acceptable and cheaper. As the SSA, who gets the award?

options.label: Award to AeroDyne — the operational superiority justifies the premium.
Award to GlobalTech — save the $43M; Acceptable is good enough.

feedback.aerodyne_tradeoff: Best value, properly documented. Under a tradeoff you may pay a premium for a higher-rated offer — as long as the SSDD gives the rationale for why the non-cost benefits are worth the added price. You did.
feedback.aerodyne_lpta: Fatal inconsistency. Back in Phase 1 you set an LPTA strategy — which forbids paying more for higher-rated performance. Awarding to the pricier offeror now contradicts your own solicitation and guarantees a sustained protest.
feedback.globaltech_tradeoff: Defensible, but risky. Awarding to the lowest price under a tradeoff strategy can look like a disguised LPTA. If the higher-rated proposal isn't selected, the SSDD must document why its advantages weren't worth the premium.
feedback.globaltech_lpta: Consistent with your strategy. Under the LPTA process you set in Phase 1, the award goes to the lowest-priced technically acceptable offeror.

cites.quote: If a higher priced offer is selected, there must be rationale as to why payment of a higher price is justified by the beneficial positive aspects of the proposal in the non-cost factors.
The SSA shall not merely rely on the adjectival ratings alone.

verdicts.headline: Award successful — an ironclad source selection.

verdicts.body: The award would likely stand, but you left the Government exposed on at least one call. Review the log below and see where the risk crept in.

verdicts.headline: Protest sustained — major errors committed.
